note.p: Thomas Gwennap, son of the Reverend Joseph Gwennap. It seems that William Godwin's father, the Reverend John Godwin of Guestwick, was a member of the Society for Propagating Religious Knowledge which he joined in 1767. Joseph Gwennap was also a member of that society. It was a well known dissenting organisation for publishing books for the poor. Joseph's uncle was Andrew Gifford who attended Samuel Jones' seminary in Tewkesbury alongside Edward Godwin, (William Godwin's grandfather). Gifford established a church in Holborn and Joseph attended that church. Joseph died in 1813 and the diary entry is for 1814 which makes it likely that it was his son Thomas in the diary. He lived in Piccadilly and was as an art-dealer. The name Gwennap is very rare in London, (common in the west country). Thomas Gwennap married the daughter of John Godwin of the Strand. It turns out that Joseph Gwennap opened his own baptist church in Piccadilly from 1783-1798. It was directly across the road from the home of the king's dentist, Charles Dumergue. Dumergue loaned John £200 against his life insurance policy in 1800. What is also of passing interest is that Sir Walter Scott lived with Dumergue and met William Godwin through Charles Lamb. So John and William Godwin shared the mutual acquaintance of Hesther Piozzi and Samuel Lysons, and both families were associated with the Gwennaps. William met with one of the Burneys on that same day and John Godwin of the Strand published a book with illustrations by Edward Burney. His Cousin Frances Burney was keeper of the robes for Queen Charlotte and was a good friend of Hesther Piozzi, who wrote letters to Samuel Lysons when he was living with John in the Strand. I think that having Burney do the illustrations for his pocketbook may explain how John Godwin managed to get his royal charter as pocketbook maker to the Prince of Wales.
